einzeiler: How the controversial model of Moscow, Idaho, inspires Christian nationalist projects.
kurzfassung: Residents in Gainesboro look to Moscow, Idaho, as a blueprint after venture-backed developers target their town for a Christian nationalist community. Led by Pastor Doug Wilson, Christ Church spent decades deeply dividing Moscow through schools, businesses, and ideological real estate acquisitions. While Wilson views Moscow as a successful model for national transformation, local residents are now organizing to buy property and push back.
stichpunkte: Christ Church in Moscow, Idaho, has spent fifty years attempting to establish a society under biblical law.
Pastor Doug Wilson embraces the label of Christian nationalist and promotes patriarchal and absolutist social structures.
The church expanded its influence by founding private schools, a college, publishing houses, and acquiring prominent downtown real estate.
Despite significant economic and social impact, Kirkers remain a political minority and have largely lost local elections.
During the COVID-19 pandemic, Wilson openly defied public health mandates, transforming local perception of the church from a strange quirk into a direct threat.
Local residents in Moscow have begun organizing investment groups to purchase real estate and prevent further church expansion.
Developers behind the Ridge Runner project in Gainesboro, Tennessee, explicitly look to Moscow as a prototype for their own planned community.
Doug Wilson expresses skepticism toward younger radical right figures involved in new town projects, warning they will attract weirdos.

kapitel.titel: Provoking Conflict and Building an Educational Empire
Walking Main Street with Doug Wilson
Pandemic Defiance and Real Estate Countermeasures
Exporting the Moscow Model to Tennessee

clips.hook: A town divided by denomination and coffee shops
clips.text: Gainsborough residents examine the situation in Moscow to anticipate how a local developer might transform their area, inspiring Diana to consider resistance tactics.

clips.hook: Absolutist ideology and prescriptive rules for daily life
clips.text: Pastor Wilson explains why he embraces the term Christian nationalist over harsher accusations like white supremacy, arguing that civil authority should follow biblical principles.

clips.hook: Admitting failure in local political races
clips.text: Church affiliates steadily acquired historic downtown real estate to house their private academies and eateries, catching long-time locals off guard.

clips.hook: Organic growth through large families instead of a military takeover
clips.text: Advertisements spotlight Elizabeth Smart's show dedicated to survival stories, followed by a preview of a weekly podcast about books and pop culture.

clips.hook: One little bacon-wrapped sausage as an indicator of a larger project
clips.text: Wilson explains how establishing an independent service firm allowed his group to navigate municipal resistance, pointing to thirty acres of eastern land secured for church expansion.
